title: Factors affecting membrane permeability; Specific immune response: antigens and lymphocytes; Vaccination and herd immunity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: MB05#t2 term and clue written for the game; MB05#t3 term and clue written for the game; IM03#t1 term and clue written for the game; IM03#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: IM03#N.2, IM05#N.2, MB05#N.8, IM03#N.4, IM05#N.4, IM03#N.8, IM05#N.6, IM03#N.10, IM05#N.11b, IM03#N.14, IM05#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Colorimeter
items.clue: Instrument that shines filtered light through a sample held in a cuvette.

items.label: Absorbance
items.clue: Measure of how much light a sample takes up; higher when more pigment is present.

items.label: Antigen
items.clue: Molecule, often a surface protein or glycoprotein, that triggers an immune response.

items.label: T killer cells
items.clue: Lymphocytes that bind infected or cancerous targets and release pore-forming proteins.

questions.stem: Which statement about antigens is correct?

options.text: Antigens are proteins made by lymphocytes that bind to pathogens and mark them for destruction by the phagocytes.
Most antigens are glycoproteins or other proteins, usually located on the outer surface of a pathogen.
Antigens are toxins released by a pathogen into the blood, and it is these toxins that the antibodies must neutralise.
Antigens are found only on pathogens; molecules on the surface of human cells do not act as antigens.

questions.explanation: Antigens are recognition molecules that trigger antibody production. Most are glycoproteins or other proteins on the outer surfaces of pathogens, where the immune system can recognise them.

questions.stem: An mRNA vaccine against COVID-19 contains RNA with the sequence coding for the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, packaged in lipid nanoparticles. Which statement correctly explains how it stimulates immunity?

options.text: The RNA is translated into antibodies against the spike protein, which then circulate in the blood ready to bind to the virus.
Cells translate the RNA into spike protein, an antigen that stimulates the adaptive immune system to form memory cells without causing disease.
The RNA produces a weakened form of the whole virus inside the person's cells, giving a mild case of COVID-19 that generates immunity.
The RNA is copied into the DNA of the person's chromosomes, so that their cells will permanently carry and express the gene for the viral antigen.

questions.stem: A student makes a 1-in-10 dilution series: each step transfers 1.0 cm³ of the previous solution into 9.0 cm³ of distilled water. What is the concentration in the third diluted tube, as a fraction of the stock?
questions.explanation: Each step is 1.0 cm³ in a total of 10.0 cm³: ×1/10. Three steps: (1/10)³ = 1/1000.

questions.stem: Which statement about B-lymphocytes and antibodies is correct?

options.text: Each B-lymphocyte examines the antigen it meets and then adjusts the shape of the antibody it makes so that it fits the antigen.
Helper T-cells and B-lymphocytes both secrete antibodies, which is why they are said to cooperate in producing them.
A person has a very large number of different B-lymphocytes, and each of them makes a single specific type of antibody.
B-lymphocytes are found only in the blood; lymph nodes contain trapped pathogens but no lymphocytes at all.

questions.explanation: The diversity of B-cells, not any tailoring by an individual cell, is what allows a specific response to almost any antigen.

questions.stem: For measles, transmission in a population is greatly impeded once about 95% of people are immune. A community's vaccination coverage falls from 96% to 85%. Which statement correctly describes a consequence?

options.text: The unvaccinated people remain immune too, because herd immunity continues to protect the whole population permanently once it has been reached.
Only the people who chose not to be vaccinated are affected, because each person's vaccination status affects only their own risk of infection.
There is no consequence, because measles was eliminated from the community while coverage was above 95% and so cannot return.
People who are not immune, including those who cannot be vaccinated, are at greater risk because chains of transmission are no longer broken.

questions.stem: In an experiment, B-lymphocytes specific to an antigen were cultured with that antigen and no other cells. No antibody was produced. When helper T-lymphocytes were added to the culture, antibody production began. What does this show?

options.text: Binding of the antigen alone should have activated the B-lymphocytes, so the first culture must have been set up incorrectly.
The antibody in the second culture was secreted by the helper T-lymphocytes, which make antibody when they meet an antigen.
A B-lymphocyte is activated to produce antibodies only when it both binds its specific antigen and makes contact with a helper T-lymphocyte.
The helper T-lymphocytes showed the B-lymphocytes the shape of the antigen so that they could then design an antibody to fit it.

questions.stem: A person had influenza last winter and recovered fully. This winter they catch influenza again. Which is the best explanation?

options.text: Last winter's antibodies have been broken down, and immunity depends on keeping those antibodies.
Their phagocytes have forgotten the virus since last winter.
The virus's surface antigens have changed, so their memory cells' receptors are no longer complementary.
Memory cells survive for only a few months, so none were left by this winter.

questions.explanation: Antigen variability: this year's strain is not recognised by last year's memory cells, so a slow primary response is needed again.

questions.stem: After a person is exposed to a new pathogen for the first time, several days pass before antibodies against it can be detected in the blood. Which statement best explains this delay?

options.text: A single activated B-cell can make all of the antibody required, but several days are needed for one cell to synthesise and secrete that much protein.
Few B-cells are specific to the antigen; after activation they must divide by mitosis to form a clone of plasma cells before enough antibody is made.
The activated B-cells must first divide to produce plasma cells that make a range of different antibodies, and it takes days to make a set that fits the pathogen.
The B-cells need several days to study the antigen and modify their antibody genes until the antibody they make fits the antigen's shape.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is valid from the trial data in N.10?

options.text: In this trial, vaccinated adults had about 95% fewer cases of symptomatic COVID-19 than those given the placebo.
The vaccine protects 95% of people for life.
The vaccine caused COVID-19 in the 8 vaccinated people who became ill.
Only 8 of 18 198 vaccinated people became ill, so the vaccine is 99.96% effective.

questions.explanation: Efficacy compares the two groups' risk: (0.44 − 8.84) ÷ 8.84 × 100 = −95%.

questions.stem: A child is born with no T lymphocytes. Her B lymphocytes are normal in number and type. Why does she make very little antibody against most pathogens?

options.text: T lymphocytes normally secrete most of the body's antibodies, so without them little antibody is made.
B cells need T cells to show them the antigen's shape, so that they can then design an antibody to fit it.
This should not happen: a B cell starts making antibody as soon as it binds its antigen.
B cells that bind antigen are not activated without T helper cells, so no plasma cells form.

questions.stem: A news article reports a newly published study claiming that a vaccine causes a rare side effect, before other scientists have evaluated the study. Which response shows the best understanding of how science works?

options.text: Accept the claim as established, because a study that has been published in a scientific journal has been proven to be correct.
Conclude that the vaccine is unsafe, because a vaccine that is genuinely safe would carry no risk of side effects of any kind.
Treat the claim as provisional until other scientists have evaluated the study; vaccine risks are minimal but not nil.
Dismiss the claim without reading it, because vaccines are tested so rigorously that a side effect of any kind is impossible.
